locke-personal-identity: John Locke argued that what makes a person the same individual over time is not the persistence of a soul or a body but the continuity of consciousness, especially memory. On this view, a person is a thinking, self-aware being who can regard itself as the same across different times and places, and identity extends only as far as that consciousness can reach back through remembered experience. The theory reframes selfhood as a psychological rather than a metaphysical fact, and it raised enduring puzzles about lapses of memory, forgotten deeds, and the boundaries of moral responsibility.
tabula-rasa: Tabula rasa, Latin for a blank slate, is the doctrine that the mind at birth contains no innate ideas and that all knowledge derives from experience. John Locke advanced it against rationalists who held that certain principles are stamped on the mind from the start, arguing instead that sensation and reflection furnish the raw materials of thought. The view makes experience the ultimate source of concepts and became a cornerstone of British empiricism, with far-reaching implications for education, moral development, and the shaping of human character.
locke-natural-rights: Natural rights are entitlements that individuals possess by virtue of their humanity rather than by the grant of any government. John Locke held that in a state of nature persons hold rights to life, liberty, and property that precede political authority, and that the legitimate purpose of government is to protect these rights by consent of the governed. The idea supplied a standard against which states could be judged and justified resistance to rulers who violated it, deeply influencing later liberal and revolutionary political thought.
locke-labor-property: The labor theory of property holds that a person acquires a rightful claim to a previously unowned thing by mixing their labor with it. John Locke reasoned that although the earth is given to humanity in common, each individual owns their own body and its work, so gathering, cultivating, or fashioning something makes it one's own. He qualified this with provisos that one should leave enough and as good for others and not let goods spoil, offering an early attempt to justify private property from within a framework of natural rights.
berkeley-idealism: Subjective idealism, captured in the maxim esse est percipi, to be is to be perceived, is the view that physical objects have no existence independent of being perceived by a mind. George Berkeley argued that we are only ever acquainted with our own ideas and sensations, so it is incoherent to posit unperceived material substance behind them; what we call things are simply stable collections of sensible qualities. To explain why the world persists when no human observes it, he held that all ideas are continuously perceived by the infinite mind of God, making reality fundamentally mental rather than material.
hume-is-ought: The is–ought problem observes that arguments frequently slide from statements about what is the case to conclusions about what ought to be, without explaining how the shift is warranted. David Hume noted that a purely factual or descriptive premise cannot by itself entail a prescriptive or moral conclusion, since the terms of obligation appear only in the conclusion and nowhere in the premises. The point challenges attempts to derive morality directly from natural facts and has framed much subsequent debate in ethics about the gap between fact and value.
hume-induction: The problem of induction concerns whether we are ever justified in inferring from observed cases to unobserved ones, such as expecting the future to resemble the past. David Hume argued that such inferences rest on a presumption of the uniformity of nature that can be established neither by logic, since no contradiction follows from denying it, nor by experience, since that would already assume the very principle in question. He concluded that inductive expectation is grounded in habit and custom rather than rational demonstration, a skeptical result that continues to shape the philosophy of science.
hume-bundle: The bundle theory of the self denies that there is any persisting, unified substance underlying our mental life. Examining his own experience, David Hume found only a succession of particular perceptions—sensations, feelings, and thoughts—but no impression of a simple, continuous ego to which they belong. He therefore proposed that the self is nothing more than a bundle or collection of these fleeting perceptions, held together by relations such as resemblance and causation, a conclusion that unsettles ordinary assumptions about a stable inner subject.
hume-sentimentalism: The claim that reason is, and ought only to be, the slave of the passions expresses David Hume's view that reason alone cannot move us to act or set our ends. Reason, on his account, discovers facts and traces relations of ideas, but it is desires, feelings, and aversions that supply motivation; reason serves by finding the means to satisfy passions it does not itself generate. This sentimentalist position locates the springs of action and the foundations of morality in human feeling rather than in pure rationality.
hume-miracles: In his essay on miracles David Hume argued that no testimony can rationally establish that a miracle has occurred. Since a miracle is by definition a violation of a law of nature supported by uniform and extensive experience, the evidence against it is as strong as evidence can be, whereas human testimony is often mistaken or deceptive. Hume concluded that a wise person should believe a miracle report only if its falsehood would be even more improbable than the event it describes, a standard he thought testimony could rarely if ever meet.
reid-common-sense: Common sense philosophy is the position that certain basic beliefs—in the existence of the external world, other minds, and the general reliability of our faculties—are foundational principles we are entitled to accept without proof. Thomas Reid developed it in direct response to the skeptical conclusions of Hume, arguing that a philosophy which ends by denying what everyone unavoidably believes has gone astray in its premises rather than uncovering the truth. He held that these first principles are built into the constitution of the mind and that trusting them is a mark of sound reasoning, not credulity.
categorical-imperative: The categorical imperative is Immanuel Kant's supreme principle of morality, a command of reason that binds unconditionally rather than depending on any desired end. In its central formulation it directs one to act only on that maxim which one could at the same time will to become a universal law, testing whether the principle behind an action could be consistently adopted by everyone. Kant contrasted it with hypothetical imperatives, which tell us what to do only if we happen to want some goal, and made it the rational ground of moral duty.
kant-humanity-formula: The humanity formula is one of Immanuel Kant's expressions of the categorical imperative, requiring that we treat humanity, whether in ourselves or in others, always as an end and never merely as a means. Because rational beings possess an intrinsic worth, or dignity, that is not exchangeable for any price, they must never be used simply as instruments for someone else's purposes. The principle grounds duties such as honesty and respect and has become a touchstone for arguments about human dignity and the wrongness of manipulation and coercion.
kant-autonomy: Autonomy of the will is Immanuel Kant's idea that the moral law is one that a rational agent gives to itself rather than receives from any external source. To be autonomous is to legislate universal principles through one's own reason and to act from them out of duty, so that genuine freedom consists in self-governance according to moral law rather than in doing whatever one is inclined to do. Kant contrasted this with heteronomy, in which the will is determined by desires or outside authority, and made autonomy the basis of both moral obligation and human dignity.
kingdom-of-ends: The kingdom of ends is Immanuel Kant's ideal of a moral community in which all rational beings are united under common laws that each of them legislates and to which each is subject. Every member is at once a lawgiver and one who obeys, and each is treated as an end in themselves possessing dignity rather than a mere means. Kant offered this vision as a further formulation of the categorical imperative, inviting us to act as though we were always legislating for such a systematic union of rational agents.
